specPoints.text: CORE PRACTICAL 3 Finding the concentration of a solution of hydrochloric acid.

primer.text: A burette plus a standard solution can price an unknown acid. This note runs the titration routine - dropwise discipline, half-division readings, concordant titres - then converts the averaged titre through the one-to-one equation into the hydrochloric acid concentration, worked end to end.

lessons.title: Running the titration with precision
lessons.opening: Core Practical 3 finds the concentration of hydrochloric acid by titrating it against a standard sodium hydrogencarbonate solution. This lesson assembles the burette, pipette and indicator routine, and states the reading precision and the dropwise discipline that make the end point trustworthy.
keyPoints: The burette is the key instrument, marked to 0.10 cm3 and read to a half-division uncertainty of plus-or-minus 0.05 cm3.
The end point, when the two solutions have reacted completely, is shown by an indicator's colour change.
A measured aliquot of one solution goes into the conical flask with indicator, and the other solution runs in from the burette.
Near the end point the flow slows to dropwise addition, closing the tap after one drop flips the colour.
A white tile under the flask makes the colour change easy to see, and repeated runs are taken until concordant results within 0.1 cm3 emerge.

low.restatement: Pipette the aliquot, fill the burette, add indicator, and run the titrant in fast at first then dropwise as the colour starts to turn; stop on the single drop that completes the change and read the burette to the half division.
low.analogy: Parking a car: fast in the open road, then inch-by-inch into the tight space - the last drop is the handbrake moment.
low.examPointer: Quote the 0.05 cm3 reading uncertainty and the 0.1 cm3 concordance band whenever precision is examined.

medium.restatement: The end point is a stoichiometric event dressed as a colour event: the indicator signals that the mole counts have just balanced, so overshooting by two drops corrupts the titre; dropwise control plus the white tile keeps the signal sharp and readable.
medium.analogy: A balanced see-saw tips visibly with one extra coin; the indicator is the fulcrum that announces the balance point.
medium.examPointer: Explain the white tile and dropwise stages together as the machinery of a sharp, reproducible end point.

check.stem: To what precision should burette readings be recorded?

options.text: To plus-or-minus 0.05 cm3, half the smallest 0.10 cm3 marking
options.explanation: Analogue instruments are read to half a division, so each burette reading carries the 0.05 uncertainty.
That discards the instrument's real precision.

options.text: To plus-or-minus 0.10 cm3 for each reading
options.explanation: 0.10 is the division size; the reading uncertainty is half of it.
No burette supports that claimed precision.

check.stem: What marks the end point of the titration?

options.text: The indicator's colour change showing the solutions have just reacted completely
options.explanation: The indicator signals the equivalence of mole counts as a visible flip.

options.text: The burette reaching the zero mark
options.explanation: Zero is the starting fill, not the end point.

options.text: The first drop leaving the burette
options.explanation: The end point comes after many millilitres, not the first drop.
No gas forms in this acid-base titration.

check.stem: Why is the burette flow slowed to dropwise near the end point?

options.text: One drop can flip the indicator, so dropwise addition prevents overshooting the end point
options.explanation: Fine control keeps the titre at the true equivalence volume.

options.text: The burette tap jams if opened fully
options.explanation: The tap works freely; the reason is chemical control.

options.text: Fast flow heats the conical flask
options.explanation: Flow speed has no heating effect.

options.text: The indicator only works in darkness
options.explanation: Lighting is irrelevant; the tile brightens visibility.

check.stem: Concordant titres are defined as results within

options.explanation: Runs agreeing within 0.1 cm3 are averaged; others are discarded.
That band is ten times too loose.
That band is tighter than the instrument's precision.
The 0.1 cm3 convention is standard.

check.stem: The white tile under the conical flask serves to

options.text: Make the indicator's colour change easier to see against a plain background
options.explanation: The tile's white surface sharpens the visual end point.

options.text: Keep the flask warm during the titration
options.explanation: The titration runs at room temperature; the tile is not a heater.
Spills are mopped up; the tile's role is optical.
No electrical role exists.

check.stem: State the uncertainty carried by a single burette reading and by the titre.
check.modelAnswer: A single reading carries plus-or-minus 0.05 cm3, and the titre, being the difference of two readings, carries plus-or-minus 0.10 cm3.

check.stem: Describe how the aliquot is measured and delivered into the flask.
check.modelAnswer: A volumetric pipette measures a known volume, usually 20 or 25 cm3, of one solution into the conical flask, with indicator added as drops.

check.stem: Explain why the titre's uncertainty is double the single-reading uncertainty.
check.modelAnswer: The titre is the difference of two burette readings, and uncertainties add when quantities are subtracted, so plus-or-minus 0.05 on each reading propagates to plus-or-minus 0.10 on the difference.

check.stem: A student records final readings of 22.30, 22.40 and 25.80 cm3 against initial 0.00. Identify the concordant titres and the outlier to discard.
check.modelAnswer: The 22.30 and 22.40 titres agree within 0.1 cm3 and are averaged; the 25.80 titre sits far outside the band and is discarded as the outlier.

lessons.title: Recording titres and computing the acid concentration
lessons.opening: The numbers turn into the answer through a four-step calculation: average the concordant titres, convert the standard solution's titre to moles, transfer the moles through the one-to-one equation, and divide by the aliquot volume. This lesson works the full pipeline on the hydrogencarbonate data.
keyPoints: Both initial and final burette readings are recorded to the plus-or-minus 0.05 cm3 precision.
The titre is calculated to an uncertainty of plus-or-minus 0.10 cm3 because two readings combine.
Concordant results are averaged and non-concordant ones discarded before calculation.
Moles of the standard solution equal titre volume in dm3 multiplied by its concentration.
The 1:1 stoichiometry of NaHCO3 with HCl transfers the mole count, and dividing by the aliquot volume gives the acid concentration, 0.182 mol dm-3 in the worked data.

low.restatement: Average the agreeing titres, multiply that volume in dm3 by the standard's concentration for moles, carry the moles across the 1:1 equation to the acid, and divide by the aliquot in dm3; round only at the end, to three significant figures.
low.analogy: A four-leg relay where each runner (average, moles, ratio, division) passes exactly one baton; dropping the unit conversion on leg one spoils the finish.
low.examPointer: Show the working with units at every stage and quote the final concentration in mol dm-3 to three significant figures.

medium.restatement: The processing law is stoichiometric bookkeeping: the standard solution's known concentration prices its moles, the equation's ratio converts currency between the two reagents, and the aliquot volume converts moles back into the unknown concentration - precision flows through the chain only as well as the titre that starts it.
medium.analogy: Converting money abroad: a known exchange rate (the equation ratio) turns one currency's amount (the standard's moles) into the other's (the acid's moles).
medium.examPointer: Identify the 1:1 ratio explicitly from the equation before transferring moles, since any other ratio would need scaling first.

check.stem: The average titre in the worked data is 22.80 cm3. The moles of sodium hydrogencarbonate delivered equal

options.explanation: Volume in dm3 times concentration yields moles directly.

options.text: 22.80 x 0.200, treating the titre as dm3
options.explanation: The volume must be divided by 1000 first.
Moles come from volume times concentration, not the inverse.
That returns a dm3 per mol quantity, not moles.

check.stem: The ratio NaHCO3 : HCl in the equation is 1 : 1, so the moles of hydrochloric acid in the aliquot are

options.explanation: A one-to-one equation passes the mole count across unchanged.
Doubling would need a 1:2 coefficient pattern.
Halving would need a 2:1 pattern.
The equation supplies the ratio, so the count transfers fully.

check.stem: The hydrochloric acid concentration computes to

options.text: 0.182 mol dm-3, the moles over the 0.0250 dm3 aliquot
options.explanation: Moles divided by the aliquot volume give the concentration to three significant figures.
That is the hydrogencarbonate's concentration, not the acid's.

options.text: 1.82 mol dm-3, ten times too high
options.explanation: A factor-of-ten slip in the volume conversion.

options.text: 0.0182 mol dm-3, ten times too low
options.explanation: Another factor-of-ten slip, in the opposite direction.

check.stem: Why are non-concordant titres discarded before averaging?

options.text: Runs outside the 0.1 cm3 band carry systematic or technique error that would bias the average
options.explanation: Only mutually agreeing titres indicate reliable technique, so the average uses those.
Simplicity is incidental; validity drives the discard.

options.text: Because the burette changes between runs
options.explanation: The burette is the same instrument throughout.

options.text: Because all titres must be identical by law
options.explanation: Variation is normal; the band defines acceptance.

check.stem: Recording initial and final burette readings to the stated precision means writing values such as

options.text: 0.00 and 22.80 cm3, both to two decimal places
options.explanation: Readings carry the 0.05 cm3 precision, hence two decimals.
Whole numbers discard the required precision.
Three decimals overstates the instrument.
That misplaces the decimal in the uncertainty.

check.stem: State the four steps from titres to acid concentration.
check.modelAnswer: Average the concordant titres, convert the standard's titre to moles, transfer moles through the equation ratio, and divide by the aliquot volume.

check.stem: Write the equation for the reaction used in this core practical.
check.modelAnswer: NaHCO3 + HCl gives NaCl + H2O + CO2, a one-to-one reaction between hydrogencarbonate and acid.

check.stem: Explain why the standard solution's known concentration is the anchor of the whole calculation.
check.modelAnswer: Every downstream number derives from the one quantity known exactly - the standard's concentration prices its moles, the ratio converts them, and the aliquot division finishes the chain, so an uncertain standard would corrupt everything.

check.stem: A titre of 20.00 cm3 of 0.200 mol dm-3 hydrogencarbonate reacts with a 25.0 cm3 acid aliquot. Compute the acid concentration, showing each step.
check.modelAnswer: Moles of hydrogencarbonate: 0.0200 x 0.200 = 4.00 x 10-3 mol; the 1:1 ratio passes them to the acid; concentration: 4.00 x 10-3 / 0.0250 = 0.160 mol dm-3.

glossary.definition: The volume delivered by the burette, calculated as the difference of the initial and final readings.
Titration runs that agree within 0.1 cm3 of each other and may be averaged.
The moment the indicator's colour change shows the two solutions have reacted completely.

workedExample.prompt: A 25.0 cm3 aliquot of the unknown acid meets a 0.200 mol dm-3 sodium hydrogencarbonate titrant, and the concordant titres average 22.80 cm3. Compute the acid concentration to three significant figures.
steps: Moles delivered: 22.80 / 1000, times 0.200, gives 4.56 x 10-3 mol.
The equation NaHCO3 + HCl -> NaCl + H2O + CO2 is one-to-one, so moles of HCl also equal 4.56 x 10-3 mol.
Concentration: the 4.56 x 10-3 mol sit in the 0.0250 dm3 aliquot, giving 0.182 mol dm-3.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The hydrochloric acid concentration is 0.182 mol dm-3.
